title: Sitting and forgetting
hookLine: Zhuangzi's Yan Hui "sits and forgets" everything, even himself (Zhuangzi 6)

cards: A student walks up to his teacher with news. I'm making progress, he says. I've forgotten goodness and duty.
The teacher nods. Good. But not yet.
Some days later he's back. I've forgotten ritual and music. Good, says the teacher.
But not yet. Then the student comes a third time, and this time the teacher is the one who's startled. The student is Yan Hui.

teach.b: On the third visit Yan Hui says: I sit and forget. In Chinese, zuowang. Confucius, the story says, looks startled and asks what that means.

Yan Hui answers, in plain paraphrase: I let my limbs and body drop away. I dismiss my hearing and my sight. I leave my form behind, put away what I know, and become one with the great road that runs through everything.
Then the turn. Confucius, the well-known teacher, says: if you are one with it, you have no likes; if you are changed by it, you hold nothing fixed. You really are worthy.
Please let me follow behind you.
The teacher asks to become the student. Look at the order of what gets forgotten: first goodness and duty, then ritual and music. These aren't bad things; they're the very things Confucius taught.

teach.h: EVEN THE GOOD LISTS GO DOWN.
teach.b: Yan Hui puts down even the good lists, and then the one keeping the lists. Readers take this more than one way.
Some hear a method: a real sitting practice, emptying the mind until only stillness is left, and some later Daoists took it up that way.
Others hear a joke with a point: here Zhuangzi puts words in Confucius's mouth, and lets the great teacher of rules bow to a student who has let the rules go.

teach.h: PLEASE LET ME FOLLOW BEHIND YOU.
teach.b: Either way, the story is gentle. Yan Hui doesn't fight his thoughts. He forgets them, the way you forget a coat on a warm day.

how: Readers of the Zhuangzi meet zuowang in the story of Yan Hui and Confucius, and some Daoist practitioners treat sitting and forgetting as a meditation: sitting still and letting thoughts, senses and self-concern fall away.

o: a Confucian rite of mourning for a teacher
a strict list of rules for daily meditation
sitting and letting go of body, senses and knowing

games.q: sitting and forgetting: tap the pairs.

s: in the story, Yan Hui forgets bad habits first
he forgets goodness and duty first, then ritual and music: the very things Confucius taught.
the story is told in a Daoist book, not by Confucius's followers
it comes from the Zhuangzi, which here puts words in Confucius's mouth.
Yan Hui fights his thoughts until they stop
he lets body, senses and knowing drop away. he forgets; he doesn't fight.

games.q: you're Confucius. your student Yan Hui says, I sit and forget, and explains he has let go of body, senses and knowing. what do you say?
o: scold him for forgetting your teaching.
tell him, good, but not yet.
call him worthy and ask to follow behind him.
games.why: in the Zhuangzi, Confucius says Yan Hui is truly worthy and asks to follow behind him. the teacher becomes the student.

practice: Your mind will offer a list: things to do, things you forgot, things you should have said. Don't fight it and don't finish it; just notice, a list, and set it down like a bag.
Let the body be heavy, let sounds come and go unnamed, and if another list arrives, set that one down too.

wordCard.voice: Zuowang. Sitting and forgetting, from the Zhuangzi: letting go of body, senses and knowing, until only the great road is left. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, from the Zhuangzi: sit, forget.

carryVoice: Your line: sit and forget. Nothing to achieve here, only less to carry. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Zhuangzi, chapter 6 (The Great and Most Honored Master), Yan Hui and Confucius
